post_text:
I chose a fixed-size thread pool when everyone else wanted "elastic" scaling.

It felt like I was intentionally slowing us down. 🛑

The team argued that we should let the pool grow to handle traffic spikes.

They pointed at the "429 Too Many Requests" errors as a sign of failure.

I insisted on a hard limit and a small, bounded queue.

It looked like we were leaving performance on the table.

Two years later, our main database started locking up during a migration.

Latency on the ingestion endpoint tripled instantly.

Services with elastic pools tried to spawn thousands of threads to keep up.

They hit container memory limits and entered a recursive crash loop.

Our service simply filled its queue and started rejecting new work.

The CPU stayed flat, and the JVM never broke a sweat. 🧘‍♂️

We didn't have to recover because we never actually fell over.

The "bad" metric of rejected requests was actually our shield.

What I learned:

A system that knows when to say no is more resilient than one that tries to do everything until it dies.
